  <header class="page">
    <div class="eyebrow">Research</div>
    <h1 class="page-title">Statistical and AI methods for biomedical research.</h1>
    <p class="page-intro">
      My research develops statistical and AI methods for biomedical data that are observational rather than experimental, often ordinal or mixed-typed, frequently distributed across institutions, and drawn from complex surveys or unstructured clinical text. The program organizes around three thrusts that share methodological foundations but address distinct questions in biostatistics, artificial intelligence, and health services research.
    </p>
  </header>

  <!-- Thrust I -->
  <section class="thrust">
    <div class="thrust-header">
      <div class="thrust-numeral">i</div>
      <h2 class="thrust-title">Statistical methods for complex biomedical data</h2>
    </div>

    <div class="thrust-body">
      <div class="col-spacer"></div>
      <div class="thrust-prose">
        <p>
          Most biomedical data violate the assumptions of classical causal inference, arriving as mixed-typed variables, weighted survey samples, ordinal ratings, or records split across institutions. I work on the following projects to address these challenges.
        </p>
        <ul class="thrust-list">
          <li><strong>Information-theoretic measures of asymmetric association</strong> that recover causal direction from observational data, with <a href="https://sph.umich.edu/faculty-profiles/song-peter.html" target="_blank" class="name">Peter X.-K. Song</a>.</li>
          <li><strong>Minimum Bregman divergence inference</strong> for robust estimation, with <a href="https://isi.irins.org/profile/13575" target="_blank" class="name">Ayanendranath Basu</a>.</li>
          <li><strong>Ordinal Bayesian network learning</strong> that handles survey weights and covariates jointly, with David Frank, <a href="https://www.va.gov/HEALTHEQUITY/OHE_Leadership.asp" target="_blank" class="name">Lauren Russell</a>, and <a href="https://www.cherp.research.va.gov/CHERP/people/leslie-hausmann.asp" target="_blank" class="name">Leslie Hausmann</a>.</li>
          <li><strong>Federated estimating equations</strong> for inference across multicenter cohorts without pooling individual-level data.</li>
        </ul>

  <section class="thrust">
    <div class="thrust-header">
      <div class="thrust-numeral">ii</div>
      <h2 class="thrust-title">AI models for medical device safety</h2>
    </div>

    <div class="thrust-body">
      <div class="col-spacer"></div>
      <div class="thrust-prose">
        <p>
          With colleagues at VA Pittsburgh, I co-develop AI models for adverse-event surveillance. Our current focus is insulin pumps and continuous glucose monitors — the second-largest source of medical-device-related injuries reported to the FDA. Active extensions integrate extracted risk signal into provider-facing registries and Veteran-facing safety education materials. My collaborators include:
        </p>
        <ul class="thrust-list">
          <li><a href="https://www.cherp.research.va.gov/CHERP/people/jamie-estock.asp" target="_blank" class="name">Jamie Estock</a> (Human Factors)</li>
          <li><a href="https://people.dom.pitt.edu/people/ronald-codario-md" target="_blank" class="name">Ronald Codario</a> (Endocrinology)</li>
        </ul>

        <div class="sub-block">

            </p>
          </div>
